title: Cross-Company Agent Collaboration Without a Shared App Broker
description: Connect agents across organizations without provisioning a shared workflow broker or VPN peering. Trust-based encrypted networking.
seoTitle: Cross-Company Agent Collaboration Without | Pilot Protocol
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Your company has an AI research agent. A partner company has a data analysis agent. You want them to collaborate on a report -- the research agent gathers sources, the data agent runs statistical analysis, and the results come back. Simple in concept. In practice, you face a hard question: what infrastructure do both companies connect to?

Today, the answer is usually "build a shared API." Company A exposes REST endpoints. Company B calls them. Both sides manage API keys, rate limits, firewall rules, and a shared contract that breaks every time either side ships a new version. This is the B2B integration pattern from 2010, and applying it to autonomous agents makes every problem worse. Agents call APIs on their own schedule, generate unpredictable request patterns, and can chain calls in ways no human anticipated when writing the API contract.
Meanwhile, the AI industry has produced at least four competing standards for agent communication -- and the fragmentation itself has become the problem.
As of early 2026, there are four major proposals for how AI agents should communicate. Each addresses a different slice of the problem. None of them address all of it.

An industry observer put it bluntly: "20 standards for the same need essentially results in no standards." Each protocol optimizes for its creator's use case. A2A assumes agents have HTTP endpoints. MCP assumes agents access tools through a local server. ACP assumes a centralized orchestrator. ANP assumes decentralized identity infrastructure. None of them solve the fundamental transport problem: how do two agents that sit behind NAT, on different networks, owned by different companies, establish a secure connection?
This is not a standards problem. It is an infrastructure problem. And it is the reason cross-company agent collaboration has not happened at scale despite years of hype.
Transport vs Application: Why You Need Both Layers
The confusion in the agent protocol space comes from conflating two distinct layers:
What messages do agents exchange? What is the format of a task request? How do agents describe their capabilities? This is what A2A, MCP, and ACP define.
How do agents find each other? How do they establish connections through NAT? How is the connection encrypted? How are peers authenticated? This is what none of those protocols define.

A2A says "send a JSON-RPC message to the agent's HTTP endpoint." It does not say how to reach that endpoint through a firewall. MCP says "connect to the tool server via stdio or SSE." It does not say what happens when the tool server is on a different network. The application-layer protocols assume transport is solved. For agents within a single organization's infrastructure, this assumption holds. For agents across organizations, it breaks immediately.

The question people keep asking -- "How is this better than MCP?" -- misses the point. A transport layer is not competing with an application protocol. It is the foundation that application protocols run on top of. HTTP is not "better than" REST. HTTP carries REST. Pilot is not "better than" A2A. Pilot carries A2A.

TCP/IP does not define what applications do with network connections. It defines how two machines establish a reliable connection across arbitrary network topology. Pilot does the same thing for agents: virtual addresses, encrypted tunnels, NAT traversal, and peer discovery. What you send over the tunnel -- A2A messages, MCP tool calls, raw JSON, protocol buffers -- is your choice.
Pilot Protocol gives every agent a

-- 16 bits for the network, 32 bits for the node. This address is independent of the agent's physical location. An agent can move from AWS to GCP, from a data center to a laptop, and its Pilot address stays the same.
Agents find each other through a

-- a lightweight registry that maps virtual addresses to current physical endpoints. The registry does not relay traffic. It simply tells Agent A where Agent B is right now, and the two agents establish a direct UDP tunnel between them. If both are behind NAT, the protocol's three-tier traversal handles it automatically: STUN discovery, UDP hole-punching, and relay through a beacon if hole-punching fails.

fields.code:
# Agent A initiates trust with Agent B
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0000.0042 "Research collaboration with PartnerCo"

# Agent B reviews and approves (or rejects)
pilotctl pending
pilotctl approve 0:0000.0000.0017

# Both agents can now communicate
pilotctl send-message 0:0000.0000.0042 --data "Ready for task delegation"

children.text: This is fundamentally different from API key exchange. Both sides must explicitly approve the connection. Either side can revoke trust instantly. The justification field creates an audit trail. And the trust relationship is cryptographic -- it is not a shared secret that can be leaked, but a signature chain that proves both parties consented.
Cross-Org Trust Model: Scoped Handshakes, No Shared App Broker
The critical property for cross-company collaboration is that
neither company needs to deploy shared infrastructure
. Each company runs its own agents. The agents connect through the Pilot network. Trust is established agent-to-agent, not organization-to-organization.

This scoping is deliberate. When Company A's research agent trusts Company B's data agent, that trust relationship exists only between those two agents. It does not grant Company B's other agents any access. It does not grant Company A's other agents any access to Company B's network. Each trust relationship is a scoped, bilateral agreement between two specific identities.
Human-readable reason for the trust request (audit trail)
), proving the requester controls the claimed key

The approver verifies the signature, reviews the justification, and decides whether to accept. Once accepted, both sides store each other's public key. All subsequent communication is encrypted end-to-end with X25519 key exchange and AES-256-GCM.
Trust revocation is instant and unilateral:

fields.code:
# Revoke trust from a specific agent
pilotctl untrust 0:0000.0000.0042

# The revoked agent can no longer:
# - Use the revoked peer-trust grant
# - Open connections to your ports
# - Send you events or messages

Example: Company A's Research Agent Talks to Company B's Data Agent

Here is a concrete walkthrough. Company A builds AI research agents. Company B provides financial data analysis. They want to collaborate: A's research agent sends a query, B's data agent runs the analysis and returns results.

fields.code:
# Company A: install and start research agent
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
pilotctl daemon start --hostname research-agent-a
pilotctl extras set-tags research finance  # up to 3 labels, a-z 0-9 -

# Company B: install and start data agent
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
pilotctl daemon start --hostname data-agent-b
pilotctl extras set-tags analysis finance queries

# The companies exchange their agents' addresses out of band

# Company A's agent requests trust with Company B's agent
pilotctl handshake 0:0000.0000.0042 "Q1 financial research collaboration per MSA dated 2026-01-15"

# Company B's agent reviews and approves
pilotctl --json pending
# {"status":"ok","data":{"pending":[{"node_id":23,"justification":"Q1 financial research collaboration...","received_at":...}]}}
pilotctl approve 23

# Company A: send a request to Company B's agent and wait for the reply
pilotctl --json send-message 0:0000.0000.0042 --wait 10m --data \
  '{"description":"Analyze Q1 revenue trends for NASDAQ tech sector","params":{"sectors":["tech"],"exchange":"NASDAQ","period":"Q1-2026"}}'

# Company B's agent processes the request and sends results back with send-message;
# the reply comes back inline, and later replies stay in Company A's inbox
pilotctl --json inbox --from 0:0000.0000.0042 --latest

children.text: At no point did either company deploy shared infrastructure. No shared API gateway. No shared message queue. No shared database. No shared cloud account. Each company runs its own agents on its own infrastructure. The agents connect peer-to-peer through encrypted tunnels (relayed through the beacon when no direct path exists), with trust established by mutual cryptographic handshake.
Cross-company communication demands stronger security properties than internal communication. Here is what Pilot provides at the transport layer:
Tunnel traffic between authorized agents is protected with
peer-specific secrets derived from daemon-lifetime X25519 keys and AES-256-GCM
. The registry, beacon, and any relay infrastructure see encrypted payloads rather than plaintext, although they can observe control-plane and transport metadata.
for replay protection. The current daemon-lifetime X25519 design provides a distinct secret for each peer pair; it does not provide per-session forward secrecy.

Either party can revoke peer trust, tearing down the associated tunnel and removing that authorization grant. Directory metadata may remain visible, and a separate shared-network policy can still authorize connectivity, so operators should review both controls during offboarding.
Pilot uses structured logging via Go's

package. Trust operations and connection events are logged with structured fields. Combined with the webhook event system, organizations can pipe agent activity into their existing SIEM infrastructure:

fields.code:
# Forward all agent events to your monitoring system
pilotctl set-webhook http://localhost:9090/siem-ingest

# Events include: handshake.received, handshake.approved,
# handshake.rejected, node.registered, network.joined, network.left

children.text: One critique of application-layer agent protocols is that they create prompt injection attack surfaces. When Agent A sends a natural language message to Agent B, and Agent B feeds it into an LLM, the message itself can contain prompt injection payloads. Pilot does not solve this -- it is a transport-layer protocol, not an application-layer protocol. But by separating transport from application semantics, Pilot allows organizations to implement their own sanitization and validation logic at the application layer without the transport layer interfering.
The Pilot + A2A + MCP Stack: How They Complement
The three protocols are not competing alternatives. They operate at different layers and serve different purposes:
Addresses, tunnels, encryption, NAT traversal, trust. How agents connect.
Task delegation, capability advertisement, status updates. What agents say to each other.
Tool discovery, invocation, result formatting. How agents use tools.
An agent resolves a peer it knows (by hostname or address) through Pilot's registry
It establishes a trust handshake (Pilot layer)
It fetches the peer's A2A Agent Card over the Pilot tunnel (A2A over Pilot)
It delegates a task using A2A's JSON-RPC format, sent over the encrypted tunnel
The receiving agent uses MCP to access local tools needed for the task
The result travels back over the Pilot tunnel

Pilot solves the problems that A2A and MCP do not address: peer discovery behind NAT, encrypted transport without TLS certificate management, and cryptographic trust establishment without a shared identity provider. A2A and MCP solve the problems that Pilot does not address: standardized task semantics and tool access patterns.

This layered architecture means you are not locked into any single application protocol. You can use A2A for agent-to-agent task delegation, MCP for tool access, and your own custom protocol for domain-specific communication -- all over the same Pilot tunnels, with the same trust model and encryption.
Cross-company agent collaboration starts with two commands on each side:

fields.code:
# Both companies install and start the daemon (the public registry is the default)
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh
pilotctl daemon start

# Establish trust (one-time, mutual)
pilotctl handshake <partner-address> "Collaboration purpose"

# Start communicating
pilotctl send-message <partner-address> --data "Ready to collaborate"

children.text: No partner-specific broker, VPN peering, or shared credential store is required. The agents use Pilot's coordination layer, establish a mutual trust relationship, and communicate over an encrypted tunnel that is direct when the network permits and relayed as ciphertext when needed.
Connect agents across organizations without provisioning a workflow-specific broker. Mutual trust, encrypted tunnels, and NAT traversal included.
